result.instructions:
XenoNet maps the Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build sessions on this machine, through a background service, a CLI, MCP tools and a desktop console. These tools operate installed XenoNet and development instances. Use installed for the person's app, or demo for made-up data. The service and the coordination between sessions keep running when Desktop closes or restarts. Simulation and arbitrary page execution work only in development instances.

The loop: `launch` (the demo instance, with made-up data, unless you need the user's real sessions: instance "dev"), then act with `find`, `select`, `navigate`, `command` and `input`, then `screenshot` to look. Every action waits until the view has settled (the layout cooled, the camera and any gathering at rest) and returns the new state, so don't sleep between calls. `simulate` puts sessions into rare states (a question waiting, an edit collision, a stuck loop) and has actors act. `actors` lists the actors beside the map, and `feed` reads the activity feed. After a change, check `logs` for page errors.

XenoNet Dev hot-reloads: saving under src/ reloads the page, under server/ restarts the server, under electron/ relaunches the app; the tools wait for it to come back. The window shows without taking focus, and the user may be watching it. Screenshots of the dev instance show the user's real session titles.

tools.name: launch

For development instances it returns once the app has exited, or once it's ended it if it was stuck on its way out (`killed`). The dev instance is the user's own XenoNet Dev, so quit it only when asked.

tools.name: find
tools.title: Find nodes
tools.description: Finds nodes on the map whose id, title or name contain every word of `query`: projects, sessions, Codex projects (native), folders outside the projects folder (zone), shared systems (resource), the shared context (wiki) and its pages (page), other machines of a network this one is in (host; their nodes' ids start with @<host>: and say which host), and actors beside the map (kind actor, by id, name and product). Drawn nodes come first, then the most recent, then actors. Each has its id, for select and input, and where it is on screen.

Give an id, or a query to select the best match from find. null clears the selection. A project's selection names its checkout on this machine (checkout: its id, the project it's in and whether it's confirmed there). A checkout of a project that already had one is a candidate until you confirm it, and its at.confirm is the inspector's Confirm button: the person's, a click in the window that only the demo and test instances let this console make. Returns the state once the view has settled.

tools.name: needs_you
tools.title: Needs you
tools.description: Reads the Needs you queue: everything waiting on the person, the longest wait first. That is sessions waiting on a question or a permission, actors waiting on them, programs asking to be actors and sessions' asks for an actor's gateway token. Each item has its key, kind (question, permission, actor, request, gateway, or requests: how many programs ask, in a window that can't see who), who it is (title, and the session's app or another machine's host), what it waits for, since when (or until when a request lapses), the actions that answer it and whether its row shows in the open panel. `open` and `close` show or hide the panel. `show` selects an item on the map, `open-app` opens a session in its app (where its question is answered), and `dismiss` puts a session's wait away, as the panel's buttons do; each takes the item's key and returns the state that follows. Allowing or denying a program, and writing to an actor, are the person's, so this tool does neither.

tools.description: Reads the Token use panel: about what today's work would cost at API prices, by app (costs) and by actor (byActor, and the rows the panel draws in actors), and the configured OpenRouter key's spend or its visible setup/error state. Each session counts for one actor at most: the one that reported it as a run, or started it, or started the session it came from; the rest is unattributed, including sessions the person starts. A run reported from elsewhere is counted apart, unpriced. Refresh asks for current cached provider usage and the breakdown again; actors opens (more) or folds (fewer) the actors past the first few. tools.name: network
tools.title: The network
tools.description: This machine's network across machines, as Network settings in the palette shows it: whether it's in one, its name and this machine; how this machine stands in it (link: live, off or removed, since when and why); each machine (online or since when, how this one reaches it (path), what's held for it while it's away, its agents and what waits on you, founder, window, where you're at, who may start and wake sessions there, and what its XenoNet takes), with its agents under it; the invites open, what waits for approval (proposals: each with what it does and who signed it), the members' feeds a fork froze here (frozen: each machine that signed two different entries at one place, so nothing more from it is taken), a roster mismatch, and this machine's titles-only, share-load, start and wake settings. `open` shows the panel and `join` its form. `start` opens Start a session on a machine (host, this one by default) with its folder, app, mode and prompt filled in; on a machine on its own, with none of those, it opens the form that starts a network. `add` opens Add a machine with the new machine's id (host) and whether you'll use a XenoNet window on it (window) filled in. `publish` opens Publish a service with its name, address (target), paths and the machines that may call it (hosts) filled in; `devices`, `services` and `context` show the panel at Your devices, Services or Shared context. context lists Xenolith's asks for a grant to sync over this machine's networks (asks: its context key and ALPN) and the grants you gave (grants: the networks each reaches, until when, whether it's attached); Allow (at.ctxAllow, by alpn|key, with at.ctxNet's boxes for the networks), Turn down (at.ctxDeny) and Take back (at.ctxRevoke, by ALPN) are the person's. context.spaces lists the spaces Xenolith curates while it's attached, each with its offers (moveOwner, shareNetwork with fromProject, unshareNetwork with narrowed), which at.ctxSign (by space|op|network) signs as you, with your device. The grant itself never shows: Xenolith collects it over XenoNet's socket. A machine can be in several networks: networks lists each (its id, name, this machine's host id in it, what it sees of this machine as sharing, its relays, whether it's in contact), and `pick` with network (an id) shows that one in the panel; relaysHere says how this machine's relays stand (the ones every network lists, its own, its home relay). person lists your devices (how each asks you, which is this machine's, which are revoked) and whether your identity's root key is sealed here; services, what this machine publishes. `message` opens the box that messages a session as you (to: its id, or @<host>:<id> for another machine's) with text in it. Making the join line, starting or joining a network, removing or replacing a machine, approving, unfreezing a machine's feed (at.unfreeze, by its author), revoking a device (at.revoke, then at.revokeYes), publishing (at.publish), what the shown network sees (at.shareAll, at.share by project), its relays (at.relayUrl, then at.relayAdd, or at.ownAdd for this machine's own; at.relayRemove, at.ownRemove), the settings (at.set for this machine's, at.setOn for another's), Start (session.at.send, once session.armed) and Send are the person's: clicks in the window, at the answer's at and message.sendAt, which only the demo and test instances let this console make. The join line shows once, masked: join.masked says whether it is, never the code. answers lists the answers to the starts you asked for. In XenoNet Dev, simulate net-… makes up a network to look at. Returns the network, and the state once the view has settled when something opened.

The layout, your rules and Codex's picks stay with each folder, so switching back brings them back. The demo has a second made-up folder, ~/Clients.

tools.name: simulate
tools.title: Simulate a session state, an actor acting, or another machine
tools.description: Puts sessions into states that are otherwise rare, so you can check how they look. The kinds are needs-you (a question waiting), collision (two sessions editing the same file, which needs a and b), stuck (a failing loop), wiki-write (a session writing to the shared context), turn-end, doctor (the doctor finding a problem), and clear, which undoes them all. Without session ids it picks the most recently active sessions. The actor-… kinds have an actor act instead, as an event it reports would. They are actor-spawn (it starts a session), actor-edit (it edits files in a project), actor-message (it messages a session), actor-online and actor-offline. The actor reacts, and a beam runs to what it touched. actor-request makes up a program asking to be an actor (named a, Heron by default), which waits for an Allow in the window. Its card shows in the attention strip, and actors lists it under requests. actor-needs-you has an actor (a, the first by default) wait on you with a made-up question. Its card shows in the attention strip, and its glow beats in the attention color until clear. actor-tunnel gives an actor (a) a made-up remote connection through a tunnel with an adapter connected, so the map draws its gate open between it and what it reads. actor-tunnel-down does the same with no adapter connected, so the gate is shut. actor-read sends a read through it, of node b or what it acts on, with light down the conduit and out to what it read. clear takes the tunnel away. Only the demo and test instances, whose data is made up, answer actor-request, actor-needs-you and the tunnel kinds, and actor-request's token stays out of this answer. host-offline and host-online take the id of another machine on the map as a. host-skew sets a host's clock b ms off, three minutes if b is left out. The net-… kinds make up a network across machines, with other machines' agents, for the Network panel (network), the attention strip and the message box: net-none (this machine on its own), net-founder (this machine started it; two more machines, one offline; on laptop a session waits on you with a question and another seems stuck), net-member (this machine joined; the founder is another), net-away (this machine joined, and studio, the founder, has been away for 25 minutes, with what's for it held), net-invite (an invite is open), net-mismatch (a machine sees another list of the network's machines), net-remote-waiting (an agent on another machine waits on you), net-approval (a window host that isn't the founder signed another in as a window host, which waits for an approval here) and net-frozen (laptop signed two different entries at one place in its feed, so its feed is frozen here until you unfreeze it). For net-founder and net-remote-waiting, a is the machine you're at, this one by default: what waits sounds only there, here or on another machine; and b titles-only has the other machines share titles only, so no question's text, last message or stuck reason comes from them; for net-founder, b ask has a run on laptop wait in Needs you for your Allow or Deny on a permission prompt, and b ask-env one whose command may read the run's environment, with the warning its Allow card shows. Any net-… kind but net-none takes b networks, which puts this machine in a second network, work, too, with nothing shared into it yet, or b xenolith, which has Xenolith on this machine ask for a grant to sync over the network (network context). clear ends it. Everything stays in memory, apart from actor-request. Returns what was used and the page's state after the update arrives.

a.description: A session id (find with kind session); for the actor-… kinds, an actor id (actors lists them, and the first one that isn't you is the default); for actor-request, the name it asks with; for host-…, a host's id; for net-founder and net-remote-waiting, the machine you're at.

b.description: The second session, for collision; for the actor-… kinds, the node it acts on (a session for actor-spawn and actor-message, a project for actor-edit; the session busy most lately when left out); for host-skew, milliseconds; for net-founder and net-remote-waiting, titles-only; networks, for a second network; xenolith, for Xenolith's ask for a grant.

tools.name: actors
tools.title: Actors
tools.description: The actors beside the map. They are the person at the console (You), always-on agents and actors of your own, drawn on a layer of their own above the map, with beams into the projects and sessions they act on. Each comes with its id, presence (working, idle, away, offline, unknown), status, how XenoNet knows of it (via), its product, its form and color in the theme, the node ids it beams into now and where it is on screen. The answer also has every beam drawn and the layer's time for its last frame. `requests` lists the programs waiting for an Allow in the window, each with what it asks, who asked, and whether its card is up. `gatewayAsks` lists sessions' asks for an actor's gateway token, each with the actor, who asked, whether it replaces a token, and whether its card is up. It never holds a token, since none exists until the person allows the ask, and no tool here allows one. `tokens` says how each registered actor's token stands, as the Actors panel shows it (works, expired or none, when it expires, and when it was last used, null if never), and never holds a token itself. `remote` lists remote actors' connections (a dot reading through a tunnel, say) and whether cloud access is on. For each connection it gives the actor, state, how many projects it reads, whether labels go, its data mode, expiry and whether an adapter is connected, and never a credential. Its `tunnels` says whether tunnel-client is here, and for each tunnel XenoNet can run, its tunnel id, whether a key is kept (never the key), whether it starts with XenoNet, and whether it runs and why not. `scopes` says what each registered actor's grant reaches: its sessions scope (a selector such as project:xenonet, and when it ends) and, for one allowed to answer permission prompts, its allow scope (every session or a list, the kinds of prompt, and when it ends), each null when it has none, with what the Actors panel's row says. The `tunnels` beside the beams give each tunnel's gate on the map, how open it is and where. Allowing an actor, setting or narrowing its scopes, pairing, revoking or turning on a remote connection, and keeping a tunnel's key or starting it, are the person's alone, so no tool here does any of it. The command actors opens the Actors panel for them. `select` selects an actor, as clicking it would. The camera frames it with what it acts on and the inspector shows it (null clears the selection), and the answer then includes the state once the view has settled.
